Lessons.Title: Represent Unit Fraction Multiplication
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: draw and interpret the product of two UNIT fractions in two different orders, while retaining the original unit square as the whole. The public 2021 source explicitly asks for different partitioning orders rather than just the final numerical fraction.

Warm-up: compare four equal-area grid sketches in which one selected part is marked; reason why different-looking blue parts may or may not represent the same fraction of the original unit. A Which One Doesn't Belong choice can have multiple valid justifications, so the original diagrams are not reduced to a fixed answer.

Activity 1: make an original unit square grid with three equal vertical columns and four equal horizontal rows. First take one third of the whole, then one fourth of that selected third: the overlap is exactly one of 12 equal cells. Draw the construction again with fourths first, then take one third of the fourth. Show that the two dark cells represent equal area even though partition order differs.

Activity 2 (Write an Expression): interpret the original student-facing Priya diagram rather than replacing it with a new two-grid creation task. Explain how BOTH 1/5 × 1/2 and 1/2 × 1/5 can describe its shaded region (one tenth of the SAME original square). Then inspect the SECOND source-provided shaded diagram and write a multiplication expression for THAT diagram; justify its selected equal area against its original whole rather than presuming that its shaded fraction is also 1/10. First-party 2-by-5 and 5-by-2 grids below are teaching alternatives for the Priya example, NOT replicas of the original source figures.

Assessment: Activity 1 requires TWO independently drawn unit squares, equal partitions in opposite orders and a reason both shaded areas equal 1/12. Activity 2 requires explanations of both Priya expressions and a source-specific written expression for a distinct provided shaded image, judged against that image. These constructions, the open Which One Doesn't Belong arguments and source-image interpretation require teacher review; correct numeric 1/12 or 1/10 alone is insufficient. Restricted publisher diagrams, original Student Task PDF and gated Cool-down are not claimed verified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit-fraction multiplication
KeyConcepts.Definition: One unit fraction of another unit fraction of the same whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two possible partition orders
KeyConcepts.Definition: Changing the order of two equal-area partitions need not change the selected overlap area.
KeyConcepts.Example: One of 12 equal cells is selected either way.

KeyConcepts.Title: Keep the original whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: The fraction of a fraction must ultimately be expressed relative to the first complete unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The selected 1/12 is one twelfth of the entire initial square, not one twelfth of only the first third.
KeyConcepts.Example: Compare the highlighted cell with all 12 equal full-unit cells.

WorkedExamples.Title: Quarter of a third
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 1/4 of 1/3 of a unit square.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Divide one whole into three equal vertical strips.
Choose one third, then divide that strip into four equal pieces.
Extend the row lines across the original square and count 12 equal cells.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four of the 1/12 cells make one third.

WorkedExamples.Title: Third of a quarter
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 1/3 of 1/4 of the same unit square.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Draw four equal strips and choose one.
Divide that chosen quarter into three equal parts.
Extend partitions to count 12 equal unit-square cells.

WorkedExamples.Title: Another order pair
WorkedExamples.Question: Find both 1/2×1/5 and 1/5×1/2.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Make two equal-unit 2-by-5 grids.
Shade one intersection cell in each orientation.
Count one selected region out of ten equal regions.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both are 1/10 of the original whole.
WorkedExamples.Check: One tenth can be drawn with different row/column order.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Regard the first chosen fraction as the new entire whole
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The final question asks for the fraction of the original complete square.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Extend all partition lines to the original boundary and recount the equal regions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use unequal divisions for the second stage
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fraction multiplication by visual partition requires equal-sized subpieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use equal spacings or a grid and check areas of the tiny cells.

SummaryPoints: Two different partition orders can represent the same unit-fraction product.
The area is expressed relative to the original whole.
Source diagram comparisons and drawing quality require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Multiply Unit Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal (IM K–5 2021, 5.NF.B.4.a): use rows and columns of the same original whole to connect unit-fraction multiplication diagrams, expressions and exact products. Students first read supplied images and later calculate without a diagram.

Warm-up — Estimation Exploration: How Much is Shaded? Record an estimate that is too low, about right and too high for the SOURCE shaded image. Discuss why the pictured region is MORE than (1/2) × (1/6) = 1/12 of the whole; approximate image dimensions do not justify replacing the source task with an exact guessed fraction. Teacher reviews estimates and visual reasoning.

Activity 1 — Notice Patterns in Expressions: the source A–D diagrams keep the SAME full square and FOUR equal columns while the equal rows grow 2, 3, 4, 5. One shaded cell has area 1/8, 1/12, 1/16, 1/20 respectively. Students select an actual source diagram, write an equivalent unit-fraction multiplication expression, explain the shading and DRAW their predicted next (six-row) diagram. Show (1/2)×(1/4)=(1/4)×(1/2)=1/8, and analogous 1/3, 1/4 and 1/5 rows. Independently-authored equal-area grids below model the mathematical structure but do NOT reproduce the publisher images.

Activity 2 — Write a Multiplication Equation: use the FIRST source-provided shaded image to write the multiplication equation for its actual shaded piece (do not invent its dimensions). Explain how the SECOND source diagram represents (1/5)×(1/3)=1/15 of the ORIGINAL whole, using rows and columns. Then solve (1/2)×(1/6)=1/12 and (1/4)×(1/6)=1/24; drawings may support but are not required for the last numerical subskills. Preserve MLR1 Stronger and Clearer Each Time: partners give feedback on the written diagram explanation and students revise it.

Assessment boundaries: fixed-whole equal-area products and their numeric answers can be authored for exact Practice; image-specific expression selection, open drawings, estimates, prediction justifications and revised written explanations require TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. The original publisher drawings/Student Task PDF and gated Cool-down have not been separately certified. Optional seven-row 1/28 practice is an EXTENSION, not the source's Activity 2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Grid-denominator pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: When a whole is partitioned into a equal columns and b equal rows, there are ab equal cells.
KeyConcepts.Rule: One cell has area 1/(ab) square unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction multiplication rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: One a-th of one b-th of the same whole is one (a×b)-th of that whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Changing row count
KeyConcepts.Definition: When column count remains constant and row count grows, one cell becomes a smaller fraction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare 1/8,1/12,1/16,1/20 for 4 fixed columns and increasing rows.
KeyConcepts.Example: One twentieth is smaller than one eighth.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four columns, two rows
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the shaded area of one cell in a 4-column-by-2-row unit square.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Partition the whole into 4 equal columns.
Divide each into two equal rows.
Count eight equal pieces and shade one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make a row-count table
WorkedExamples.Question: For 4 columns and 3, 4, 5 rows, record the selected one-cell area.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Count 4×3=12 equal cells when there are three rows.
Count 4×4=16 when there are four rows.
Count 4×5=20 when there are five rows.
WorkedExamples.Check: All numerators are one; denominators grow by four with each row.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2: explain one fifth of one third
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain why the source's 1/5 × 1/3 grid represents 1/15 of the original unit square.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count the source diagram's equal columns and rows; use a newly authored 5-by-3 model as a mathematical reference, not as the publisher figure.
Steps: Fix the original whole as one complete square.
Partition into five equal parts in one direction and three in the other.
One of fifteen equal cells is one fifteenth of the original whole; justify against the source picture.
WorkedExamples.Check: (1/5) × (1/3) = 1/(5 × 3) = 1/15; the source image explanation is teacher-reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2: one half of one sixth
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the number that makes 1/2 × 1/6 = ? true.
WorkedExamples.Method: Exact unit-fraction denominator product, optionally supported by a two-row six-column diagram.
Steps: Hold the complete unit as the original whole.
Count 2 × 6 = 12 equally sized pieces.
The product is one of twelve equal pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2: one quarter of one sixth
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the number that makes 1/4 × 1/6 = ? true.
WorkedExamples.Method: Exact unit-fraction denominator product; the diagram is optional for the numerical answer.
Steps: Hold the complete unit as the original whole.
Count 4 × 6 = 24 equal cells.
One selected part is one twenty-fourth of the whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension: predict seven rows (not original Activity 2)
WorkedExamples.Question: EXTENSION ONLY: a full unit square has 4 equal columns and 7 equal rows. What area is one equal cell?
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Count 4×7 equal cells.
Select one cell of the same size as the others.
Write the unit-fraction area relative to the whole.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The whole grid count is rows times columns, not their sum.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explicitly draw and count the rectangular array.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Think more rows means a larger cell
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The same whole is split into more equal pieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare one shaded part to the fixed-size whole square.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the source's approximate estimation image as an exact prescribed 1/4 height
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original warm-up asks for bounds and compares the shading against 1/2 × 1/6; its publisher diagram dimensions were not independently verified.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the original teacher warm-up language and review the estimate qualitatively.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace source Activity 2's 1/5 × 1/3 image and 1/2 × 1/6, 1/4 × 1/6 equations with a 4 × 7 extension
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This omits distinct source tasks and confuses extension with the required lesson.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Retain all three source expressions and treat 4 × 7 as additional practice only.

SummaryPoints: Four fixed columns with 2–5 rows yield 1/8, 1/12, 1/16, 1/20; predict six rows as source pattern continuation.
Source Activity 2 includes explaining 1/5 × 1/3 = 1/15 and calculating 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12 and 1/4 × 1/6 = 1/24.
Estimation from the source shaded image, source-image-to-equation, partner explanations and drawings remain teacher-reviewed.
Publisher gated Cool-down, independent Student Task PDF and original image binaries/rights unverified; first-party diagrams below do not claim publisher pixel parity.

Lessons.Title: Situations about Multiplying Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: represent a UNIT fraction of a NON-UNIT fraction in a realistic spatial context, then connect the labeled diagram to its multiplication expression. The 2021 source uses a sports-area fraction of a park, followed by a further fractional allocation; original pictures not copied.
Warm-up: mentally halve several unit fractions, such as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/5, explaining the full original whole. Notice that half of one fifth is one tenth, not one seventh.

Activity 1 — first-party community garden: 3/5 of a community square is reserved for gardens and 1/2 of the garden portion is for flowers. Draw a rectangle partitioned into five equal columns. Shade three columns for the garden, then split those three columns in half horizontally and identify the flower portion. Extending cuts to all five columns gives ten equal-area cells, three of which are flowers; the fraction of the full park is 3/10.

Activity 2: create a second plausible land-use story with a two-thirds allocation followed by one-fourth of that section; draw twelve equal cells and identify two of them, or 1/6 of the entire whole. Partner explains how the fraction operator acts on only the initially selected region, not the whole.

Assessment boundary: the original source asks learners to draw and explain the park situation, and some different valid partition orientations are expected. The initial and subsequent selections, consistent whole and final symbolic expression are teacher-reviewed; a single 3/10 numeric answer does not certify the drawing. Copyrighted source artwork and gated Cool-down are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction of a non-unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: A selected fraction may be subdivided into equal pieces and only some of those pieces chosen.
KeyConcepts.Example: Half of three fifths is three tenths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Contextual original whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: The final fraction refers to the entire park or unit, not just the middle-stage region.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Always distinguish 'fraction of gardens' from 'fraction of whole park'.
KeyConcepts.Example: Half the garden portion of 3/5 park is 3/10 park.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use a labeled area model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Partition in one direction for the first fraction and another for the second.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The overlap counts shaded equal cells over all equal cells of the initial region.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 of ten equal park cells are flower area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Flowers in a community park
WorkedExamples.Question: Three fifths of a park is garden; half the garden is flowers. What fraction of the full park is flowers?
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Draw a whole square divided into five equal columns.
Shade three garden columns and subdivide them into halves.
Extend the horizontal midline across the park and count three of ten equal cells.
WorkedExamples.Check: (1/2)×(3/5)=3/10; teacher checks that the drawing uses the original whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Another nested allocation
WorkedExamples.Question: Two thirds of a parcel is play area; one quarter of play area is for soccer. What fraction of the whole is soccer?
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Divide the full parcel into thirds and select two parts.
Quarter each selected third; extend lines through all thirds.
Count two out of twelve equal whole-parcel pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish the two wholes
WorkedExamples.Question: If 3/5 of the park is gardens, does 'half the gardens' equal 1/2 of the whole park?
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Name the full park as the original whole.
Find the garden fraction 3/5 and take one half of it.
Compare 3/10 with 1/2 of the full park.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; it is 3/10 of the full park.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use half the whole instead of half the selected portion
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The operation is applied to the intermediate fraction, not the full unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Shade the original allocation first, then subdivide only that portion.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the second selected portion as a different full unit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Final fraction must refer to the original entire park.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Continue all grid lines across the original whole and count every equal cell.

SummaryPoints: Represent contextual fractions in stages using a constant unit whole.
One half of three fifths is three tenths of the original whole.
Source geometry and learner explanation are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Multiply a Unit Fraction by a Non-unit Fraction
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: calculate products of a UNIT fraction by a NON-UNIT fraction through progressively more shaded equal-area rectangles. Each expression must correspond to a model; the 2021 source changes the number of shaded cells and asks learners to explain how the value is related to unit-fraction products.

Warm-up: estimate a shaded region about half a unit long and more than half-unit wide. Reason that the area should exceed one quarter square unit if both extents truly are above one half; approximate sketches do not yield an exact value until dimensions are supplied.

Activity 1: start with one whole unit square divided into four equal rows and five equal columns. Shade the first, second and third cells of exactly one row; the whole has 20 cells, three shaded. Write (1/4)×(3/5)=3/20, or 3×((1/4)×(1/5))=3×1/20.

Activity 2: compare areas when one fourth is multiplied by 1/5, 2/5, 3/5 and 4/5. The corresponding shaded pieces are 1, 2, 3 and 4 out of twenty, while the whole and size of each piece stay fixed. Predict five fifths for the full row and explain why 1/4 results, not 1/20.

Assessment boundary: matching expressions, progressive shade patterns and exact calculations can be mathematically checked, but the source's actual diagrams, constructed models and partner explanations remain teacher-reviewed. No publisher figures or gated learner responses are copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction of several equal parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Taking 1/a of b/c selects b of the ac equal whole-unit cells.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeated unit-product reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: The non-unit numerator counts how many identical unit-fraction products are selected.

KeyConcepts.Title: Progressive shading
KeyConcepts.Definition: With one fixed denominator grid, increasing the number of selected cells increases covered area in equal increments.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For a 4×5 grid, one new cell adds 1/20 of the whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: Changing 2/5 to 3/5 in a quarter row adds 1/20.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three fifths of a quarter
WorkedExamples.Question: Find (1/4)×(3/5) using a unit square.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Divide whole into four rows and five columns.
Choose one quarter-high row and shade three of five columns in that row.
Count three shaded cells out of twenty equal parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare increasing shaded cells
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute (1/4)×(1/5), (1/4)×(2/5), (1/4)×(3/5).
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Keep the whole as the same 4×5 grid.
Mark one, two or three cells in one selected row.
Record the increasing parts of the full twenty-cell unit.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each increases by exactly 1/20 square unit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four fifths of one quarter
WorkedExamples.Question: Find (1/4)×(4/5).
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Partition the whole into 20 equal pieces.
Shade four of the five cells in one quarter-row.
Count four selected twentieths.
WorkedExamples.Check: Four selected twentieths make one fifth of the whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiply the non-unit numerator into the denominator
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The numerator counts selected parts; it is not another division of the whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count b highlighted cells in an a-by-c grid to obtain b/(ac).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use unequal grids for successive examples and claim a pattern
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lesson's pattern requires a fixed-size original whole and equal cells.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the same 4×5 area grid when comparing growing numerators.

SummaryPoints: Multiply a unit fraction by a non-unit fraction using a selected-cell model.
The non-unit numerator names how many equal tiny product pieces are selected.
The fixed whole and diagram-to-expression explanation are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Multiply Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: extend shaded area reasoning to multiplying TWO NON-UNIT fractions. Learners interpret several expressions for the same shaded grid region, not only an algorithmic numerator-and-denominator multiplication.

Warm-up: compare equal-area grid illustrations where the selected part may occupy several cells. Give multiple defensible Which One Doesn't Belong reasons instead of a single arbitrary visual classification.

Activity 1: create a whole square with three equal rows and four equal columns. Shade a rectangle spanning two rows and three columns. Of twelve equal whole-unit cells, six are shaded; its side lengths are 2/3 and 3/4. Explain why (2/3)×(3/4)=6/12=1/2, and why 2×3×(1/3×1/4) produces the same six small cells.

Activity 2: use a second, differently proportioned first-party 5-by-7 grid with a shaded 2-by-4 subrectangle. Its covered area is 8/35 of the whole. Partner should identify the exact side fractions, justify that 2/5×4/7=8/35, and check that neither 2/5 nor 4/7 alone describes the whole shaded area.

Assessment: the source asks learners to relate different expressions to a single shaded area and explain why factor decomposition and fractional area agree. Student-drawn regions, explanatory claims and image interpretation remain teacher-reviewed; exact numeric products are supporting tests, not complete replacement.

KeyConcepts.Title: Product of non-unit fractions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fractional rectangle covers a selected number of equal cells in the common whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Many equivalent expressions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A selected subgrid can be understood as repeated unit-cell pieces or direct factor multiplication.

KeyConcepts.Title: Diagram must match factors
KeyConcepts.Definition: The selected rows and columns determine a geometric fraction-of-fraction product.
KeyConcepts.Rule: a/b of the height and c/d of the width shade ac out of bd equal full-unit cells.
KeyConcepts.Example: 2 rows of 5 and 4 columns of 7 cover 8 of 35 cells.

WorkedExamples.Title: Six of twelve cells
WorkedExamples.Question: A unit square is partitioned into three rows and four columns, with two rows and three columns shaded. Find the area.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Find the dimensions of the shaded subrectangle: 2/3 and 3/4.
Count 2×3=6 selected cells out of 3×4=12 whole-unit cells.
Write the multiplication expression and simplify.

WorkedExamples.Title: Multiply two non-unit fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 2/5×4/7 as an area of one whole.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Divide the square into five rows and seven columns.
Select two rows and four columns.
Count eight selected cells of the 35 total.

WorkedExamples.Title: Justify different expressions
WorkedExamples.Question: Show why (2/3)×(3/4) and 6×(1/12) describe the same shaded area.
WorkedExamples.Method: A first-party exact equal-area diagram with verbal explanation and independent fraction check.
Steps: Each selected 1/12 cell comes from a 3-row by 4-column partition.
Two selected rows and three columns cover six cells.
Add six identical 1/12-square-unit areas.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks that a claimed 2×3 subgrid is a complete rectangle and that the original whole is fixed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiply only the numerators and leave the denominator unchanged
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number of whole-unit cells is the PRODUCT of both partition counts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use an equal-row/equal-column area model to count bd total pieces.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Select arbitrary nonrectangular cells while naming rectangular side fractions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A product of side fractions refers to a rectangular region with that row/column extent.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Shade a coherent a-by-c subrectangle and label the original whole.

SummaryPoints: Area grids show why numerator products count shaded cells and denominator products count total cells.
Two non-unit fractions can have a smaller product than either factor when each lies between zero and one.
